explain.say: In 1854 John Snow marked every cholera death in a London district on a map, and they clustered around one water pump. That map changed public health. Today engineers do the same kind of thinking with GIS, geographic information systems: maps as stacked layers of data. Here is a stack for planning a new water treatment plant.

explain.say: Each layer holds one kind of information. Some are vector data: points, lines and shapes, like roads and building outlines. Others are raster data: a grid of cells, each holding a value, like the elevation layer at the bottom. Which type would you use for rainfall across a whole region?

draw.verdict: Use vector for things, raster for fields

explain.say: Raster! The power comes from combining layers. A buffer draws a zone around a feature, say five hundred metres either side of a road. Overlay then keeps only land that is inside the road buffer, outside the flood zone, and gently sloping. Look at the flood zone layer: no treatment plant should sit there.

explain.say: To rank the sites that remain, use weighted overlay. Score each site from one to five on each factor and weight by importance: slope fifty percent, soil thirty, distance to road twenty. Site A scores four, three and five, giving three point nine. Look at the bars: which site wins?

Site A! Layers only line up if they share a coordinate system, such as WGS 84 or a UTM zone, so always check that first. Cities use GIS to manage every pipe, valve and road. Superb! Challenge: a site scores two for slope, five for soil and four for road access. What is its weighted score?

faq.a: A geographic information system stores, analyses and maps data tied to locations, as layers that can be overlaid, queried and combined, for planning, asset management and analysis.
asks: What is GIS used for in civil engineering?

faq.q: What is the difference between raster and vector data?
faq.a: Vector data uses points, lines and polygons for discrete features like pipes and plots. Raster data is a grid of cells with values, suited to continuous surfaces like elevation and rainfall.

faq.q: What is a buffer in GIS?
faq.a: A zone drawn at a set distance around a feature, such as 500 metres around a road or 50 metres around a river, used to find what lies near it.
Each layer is scored on a common scale and multiplied by a weight for its importance, then the layers are added to rank locations. Weights 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 on scores 4, 3 and 5 give 3.9.
asks: How does weighted overlay pick a site?

faq.q: Why do coordinate systems matter in GIS?
faq.a: Layers in different coordinate systems or datums will not line up, possibly by hundreds of metres. All data must be projected into one system, such as a UTM zone, before analysis.

facts: Roger Tomlinson led the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s and is often called the father of GIS.
The UTM system divides the Earth into 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide.

quiz.say: The weights are 0.5 for slope, 0.3 for soil and 0.2 for road access. A site scores 2, 5 and 4. What is its weighted score?
quiz.show: Weights 0.5, 0.3, 0.2; a site scores 2, 5 and 4. Weighted score?

wrong.1: That adds the scores without weights.
wrong.2: That is the plain average of the three scores.

quiz.say: Which data type suits a digital elevation model?
quiz.show: Which data type suits a digital elevation model?
quiz.why: Elevation varies smoothly, so a grid of height cells is natural.

wrong.1: Vector suits discrete features like pipes and roads.
